edition_notes: Gigamic, © 1991, from a concept of Blaise Muller; rulebook ref. QUARTO 11-2016 (multilingual; English rules on page 4). Two-player game.

items.rule: The game uses one board with 16 squares and 16 different pieces.
Each piece has 4 characteristics, each with two options: light or dark, round or square, tall or short, solid or hollow; all 16 pieces are different.
At the start, the 16 pieces are arranged at the side of the board (the board is empty).
The players throw dice (or draw lots) to decide who starts.
The first player selects one of the 16 pieces and gives it to the opponent (the starting player does not place a piece on the first turn).
The player who receives a piece must place it on an empty square of the board (any square on the first placement).
After placing, that player chooses one of the remaining unplaced pieces (15 after the first placement) and gives it to the opponent.
Play alternates this way: each turn is place the piece you were given, then choose and hand over a piece for the opponent; the player never chooses the piece they place themselves.
Objective: create a line of four pieces on the board sharing at least one common characteristic.
The line of four may be horizontal (across), vertical (up and down) or along a diagonal.
The player who places a piece completing a line must declare it by calling "QUARTO!" (and pointing out the line); without the call the win is not claimed.
A winning line is 4 light, or 4 dark, or 4 round, or 4 square, or 4 tall, or 4 short, or 4 solid, or 4 hollow pieces; several shared characteristics can accumulate in the same line.
The player calling QUARTO does not need to have placed the other 3 pieces of the line himself.
If the player who completed a line does not notice it and passes a piece to the opponent, the opponent may call "QUARTO!" at that moment, indicate the alignment, and wins the game.
If neither player notices the alignment during the move in which it is created, it loses all value and the game continues.
The game ends when a player calls "QUARTO!" and points out a valid alignment.
The game also ends when all pieces have been placed and no winner has been declared.
There is no point scoring; the game is decided by a single win condition (a called QUARTO).
The game is won by the first player to call "QUARTO!" on a valid line (including the opponent who calls it on a line the placer missed).
If all pieces are placed and no one has declared a winner, the game is a draw (even); there is no further tie-break.
A game lasts about 10 to 20 minutes; in a tournament each player may be given a time limit of 1 minute per move.
Beginner variation: play with only 1, 2 or 3 features as line criteria (e.g., a line of 4 pieces of the same colour only, one feature chosen).
Advanced variation: besides a line, a square of 4 pieces having at least one common feature also counts, giving 9 additional ways of calling "QUARTO!".
